units: sitting still for a long stretch loads the spine
the deep back muscles stiffen for want of movement
the pain comes and goes at first, then settles in for good
care providers see this trouble in adults who are younger and younger
the trouble also reaches people who have never lifted anything heavy

straightening up and moving often releases the muscular tension
adjusting the seat height keeps the thighs level with the floor
the discomfort fades within a season for those who apply these measures
text: Sitting still for hours puts far more strain on the spine than most people suspect. The deep back muscles, starved of movement, stiffen bit by bit and drag on the lower vertebrae. A dull ache sets in, coming and going at first, then settling in for good. Care providers see this complaint in adults who are younger and younger, including people who have never lifted anything heavy. The cause is rarely an injury. It lies in a slumped back, shoulders rolled forward, hips tipped backward. Putting that right costs almost nothing. Straightening up often, walking a little, stretching the muscles down the back of the legs already releases the tension that has piled up. Raising or lowering the seat so the thighs stay level with the floor finishes the job. Those who hold to this see the discomfort fade within a season.

units: the woman breaks her ankle a second time as an adult
in childhood she had worn a splint without suffering over it
as a child she kept running and laughed at her uneven walk
the adult fall happens on a slippery step
as an adult she finds her walking aid heavy and trips across the house exhausting
she understands that being still wears her out more than activity does
what made her laugh as a child shames her as an adult
a fine mark stays on her skin once the bone has knit
she takes up walking again, watching every step she places
text: The second break was nothing like the first, and that was what surprised her. As a child she had worn a light splint for a whole season without losing any of her spark: she almost ran, she hopped down hallways, she laughed at her own lopsided walk. Grown, the same joint gave way on a wet step, and the thing took on quite another color. The crutch felt heavy, the staircase hostile, the trip to the kitchen endless. She discovered that stillness wears you down more than effort ever does. What had amused her once now shamed her, not out of vanity, but because she could measure what she had stopped taking for granted. When the bone had knit, a fine scar marked the skin, a quiet trace of an ordinary fall. She learned to walk again, watching every step she placed, wary as anyone still mending.

units: the care kit is divided into three compartments
the first compartment holds the material that covers a wound
the pads must be sterile and wrapped one by one
the second compartment gathers the products spread on the skin
a soothing ointment is provided for minor burns
a gel treats bites that bring on an itch
the third compartment carries what holds or supports a limb
the expiry dates must be checked whenever the season turns
the container must be hard and kept away from heat
text: A well-built care kit sorts into three separate compartments. The first takes in whatever covers a wound: sterile pads, each one wrapped in its own sachet, adhesive dressings in several widths, a roll of tape and a pair of round-tipped scissors. The second gathers what goes onto the skin: an alcohol-free antiseptic solution, a soothing ointment for light burns, a gel for the sort of bite that brings on an itch. The third carries the holding gear: an elastic bandage, a sling, a soft splint to keep a finger or a wrist from moving at all. Check the expiry dates whenever the season turns, and throw out without hesitation anything that has already been opened. Keep the whole lot in a hard container, well away from heat and out of the reach of children, then write on the lid whatever is running low.

units: a rehabilitation center was to go up in a district that had none

the first patients taken in were coming out of major surgery
those patients often moved with a support or a device holding a limb still
a heated pool opened in the cold season that followed
the heated water serves joints that cannot bear weight on the ground
a workshop on holding the back and on preventing falls came next
that workshop is meant for older people of the area
local officials find the capacity too small and ask for an extension
text: The word went out just as the mild season opened: a rehabilitation center would go up in a working district that had never had anything of the kind before. Work began without delay inside a disused warehouse whose metal frame was left standing where it was. By autumn the first rooms were taking in patients coming out of heavy surgery, many of them leaning on a crutch or strapped into a brace. The winter that followed brought a heated pool into service, which made it possible to treat joints far too sore to bear any weight at all on the ground. Management then announced a workshop on holding the back and on preventing falls, open to the older people of the area. Local officials now hold that demand outruns the capacity that had been planned, and they are asking for the building to be made larger.

units: the heel turns red and grows slightly warm at the start
the rubbing of the shoe parts the top layers of skin
clear fluid fills the space thus opened and forms a blister
the tension of the pouch changes the way of walking
shifting the weight onto the other foot brings on a sore hip
the skin laid bare after a burst risks an infection
the area is covered with a clean pad and not opened on purpose
a thick ointment spread before walking lowers the rubbing
a final thickening of the skin makes the trouble disappear
text: The heel turns faintly red at first, a shade warmer than the skin around it. The shoe rubs it over and over, the top layers of skin part company, and clear fluid seeps into the gap that opens: a blister. Its taut roof makes standing on that foot unpleasant and alters the walk, which throws the weight onto the other foot and brings on, some time later, a sore hip. Should the pouch burst, the raw patch turns tender and lies wide open to infection. That is why it gets covered with a clean pad rather than opened on purpose. A thick ointment worked in before a long walk cuts down the rubbing that starts the whole thing off. Thin socks with no bulky seam hold the heat down as well. Once the skin thickens over that spot, it stands up better and the trouble goes away on its own.

units: the writer holds that lack of sleep is treated as ordinary
drowsiness and short temper are blamed on the load of work
sleep loss is never held responsible
evening screens push the hour of going to bed back
the stimulating drink of the next day delays the following bedtime further
the writer advises cutting the screens before entering the bedroom
the bedroom must be kept cool and dark
he recommends a steady bedtime, the end of the week included
the effects are felt after a handful of nights
sleep is presented as a repair owed and not as a privilege
text: Let us own up to it: we sleep badly, and we make our peace with that far too readily. The yawn cutting through a meeting, the heavy eyelid at mid-afternoon, the temper souring over nothing, we blame the workload for all of it, never the nights we keep cutting short. Come evening, the screen wins: one video, then another, and bedtime arrives long past the hour we had settled on. The next morning, coffee makes up the difference, pushing the following bedtime later still. Escaping that spiral involves no particular mystery. Shut the screens off before entering the bedroom, keep the room cool and dark, choose one steady bedtime, weekend included. Austere, perhaps, yet noticeable after a handful of nights. Sleep is no treat you grant yourself. It is a repair you owe yourself.

units: the physical therapist meets her patients standing, with no desk between them

the sessions there were short and the results measurable
she now practises with elderly patients in a residential district

she teaches how to get up alone and climb a staircase without fear
she works on standing steadiness in order to prevent falls
she says she enjoys this slower rhythm
her patients are after a confidence that is built one session at a time
text: The physical therapist meets each patient on her feet, at the door of her room, never from behind a desk. She started out in a hospital ward where the work was mostly injured athletes: sprains, torn muscle, a stubborn contraction after an effort nobody had prepared for. The pace ran quick there, the sessions short, the outcome easy to measure. She practises now in a residential district with elderly patients, and the trade has changed in kind. Her aim is no longer to bring a joint back to top-level sport, but to teach someone to get up off the floor alone, to climb a staircase without fear, to stand steady enough to keep from falling. She says she enjoys the slower pace of it. Where the athlete wanted a date, her patients are after confidence, and confidence gets built one session at a time.

units: the reviewer praises three aspects of the work and disputes only one
the first quality is the sharpness with which the movements are described
every handling is broken down into elementary movements with no obscure vocabulary
the second quality is the restraint of the writing

the author states when a doctor's opinion becomes indispensable
the third success lies in the hand-drawn illustrations
the reviewer finds these drawings warmer than medical photographs
the passage on muscle pain is handled too briefly
the reader closes the book pleased but slightly let down
text: This handbook of home care earns praise on three counts and objection on one. Its first strength is the sharpness of the movements it lays out: putting on a dressing, changing a pad, spotting a wound that has turned. Each handling is taken apart into elementary movements, with no murky vocabulary. Its second quality is restraint. The author marks out, without wearying of it, the limits of care given at home and the moment a doctor's opinion becomes indispensable. Its third success is a matter of beauty: the hand-drawn plates lend the volume a warmth that clinical photographs never reach. Now the objection. The chapter on muscle pain dispatches soreness and cramp in a single page, as though troubles that common deserved no study. You close the book pleased, and slightly let down.

text: I am writing to tell you what followed the operation, since you asked for the detail. It was done late last week under a local anaesthetic, and the surgeon took out the piece of bone that was jamming the joint. The next day a nurse renewed the dressing and fitted a rigid brace that I have to keep on until the follow-up visit. Over the week that followed the pain went away, though an itch came up around the stitching, the usual sign of healing according to the care team. They told me to use a plain ointment and spread it on without rubbing. Since the day before yesterday I put the foot on the ground with a single crutch, and I take the stairs leading with the sound leg. Rehabilitation will begin once the stitches are taken out. Write and tell me what your doctor makes of that schedule.

units: the night-time contraction strikes a muscle already worked in the evening
a shortage of water and mineral salts locks the muscle fibres
the episode is harmless in most cases
the attack clears in very little time
stretching the muscle by pulling the toes back stops the signal
a warm compress laid on afterwards loosens the fibre
that warmth limits the muscle soreness of the next day
drinking enough in the evening and avoiding late effort prevent a return
certain medicines that flush out water must be watched
frequent attacks that cut through sleep warrant a consultation
text: What sets off a contraction at night? The muscle seizes when it has already been worked through the evening and runs short of water and mineral salts, so the fibres lock and will not let go. Is there an illness to fear? In most cases, no: the cause stays harmless and the episode clears in a handful of moments. What can be done during the attack? Stretching the muscle gently, pulling the toes back toward the shin, stops the signal that keeps the contraction alive. A warm compress laid on afterwards loosens the fibre and limits the muscle soreness of the next day. Can a return be avoided? Drink enough in the evening, keep away from late hard effort, watch any medicine that flushes out water. When is a consultation warranted? If attacks cut through sleep and repeat without letup, an examination is in order.
